At a meeting on Monday, March 18, Piedmont City Council directed the Moraga Canyon housing project team to begin developing a specific plan for the project after narrowing the project’s options from four to two. The project’s “Option One” would keep all existing city facilities at the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue and place 130 housing units in Blair Park across the road. “Option Three” would place 130 housing units north of the skate park adjacent to the Corporation Yard and relocate the city’s corporation yard to Blair Park. During public comment, several members of the community expressed strong support for option one, while others questioned the financial implications of these projects for the city. “I’m asking [City Council] to vote for option one mainly because of fiscal responsibility,” said Jill Lindenbaum. “I think we should be prudent about our resources and realistic. Is now really the time to be building a deluxe, new soccer field?” Some residents were also concerned about the lack of integration between market rate and low-income housing units, which they believe will isolate future residents from the community. “Please distribute the income groups throughout the city so as not to create a poor neighborhood in one corner [of the city],” said community member Karen Harley. “Historically, in other parts of our country, creating a ghetto is a situation ripe for strife and contention,” she added. The discussion was spirited as community member Julie Collins took the podium for a rebuttal. “This idea of a ghetto [...] I don’t believe that’s going to happen. And we desperately need more residents. I mean, our population has almost dropped by 1,000 since 2020,” said Collins. At this meeting, the City also announced that it would seek up to 199 new housing units rather than the previously planned 132 units. The project’s initial goal was to build 60 low-income housing units and 72 market-rate units. All new housing units added to the plan would be market rate, with 60 low-income units and up to 139 potential market-rate units in total.

articles.text: In November of 2023, shortly before the beginning of Advent, my daughter called to say that she had decided to seek confirmation in the Catholic Church and that she needed a letter to the priest of the church she was joining certifying that she had been baptized in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. I responded as follows. December 2, 2023 This letter is written to confirm that Kristen Anne Phillips (Hopkins) was baptized in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit by me on Easter Sunday (April 3) 1994 in a service of public worship at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church. I am happy that Kristen (my beloved daughter) is continuing her spiritual journey by becoming part of the Roman Catholic tradition. It is truly the mother church to which she is turning. I commend her to your care. May the Peace of Advent guide us all this season. The Reverend Dr. H. James Hopkins Now, as Easter approaches, she will be confirmed on Holy Saturday, March 30, 2024. Last week we were talking about this and I told her I wanted to write about her decision and asked her to summarize the main reasons for her decision. Her answers are important. At least to me, they represent not a repudiation of religious tradition in which she was raised, but rather a testimony to the human longing for a spiritual home, a community, a tradition, a place, in which our souls can thrive. articles.text: In true community fashion, the third annual Piedmont Food Fest represents the convergence of talent, creativity, and dedication from an array of contributors, planners, partners, and sponsors motivated to deliver the most memorable festival experience on April 20 in Piedmont Park. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who have enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, and boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discoverPhotos by Meghan Bennett Last year’s attendees at the Piedmont Food Fest had a chance to meet local retailers. Emeryville Taiko performed traditional Japanese taiko drumming at last year’s Piedmont Food Fest. ing something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year’s lineup of food vendors will include fan favorites such as Robert Dorsey Catering, The Chairman, La Santa Torta, Arthur Mac’s, Satay by the Bay, and Kiss My Boba, as well as newcomers MOMOlicious, Lahore Di Khushboo, Sunrise Deli, Hila Gelato, and Annie’s T Cakes. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrant No Spices will be reprising their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. The event is free to attend and Early Bird discounts on Beer & Wine tastings as well as KidZone passes are available through March. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org for more information on this can’t-miss community experience. articles.text: The Piedmont Public Works Department has announced the opening of a new ADA-compliant access ramp in Dracena Park. Completed on March 7, the ramp provides a low-incline pathway connecting Dracena Avenue to the main body of the off-leash dog area in the park. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that the ramp is “for all intents and purposes, very usable at this point.” Community members have responded positively to the development so far. “I think this park is special,” said community member Jeff Hamm, who visits the Dracena Park off-leash dog area once a week. “I like all the trees, and my dogs really like to run around here.” Hamm mentioned that he noticed the new ramp but did not consider it an eyesore. “I think it’s a good thing that more people can access the park,” he said. Public rights-of-way and facilities are required to be accessible to persons with disabilities under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990. The city first received a request for ADA access to an offleash dog park in mid-2023. After a review of all parks in Piedmont and consulting with the city attorney, Public Works identified Dracena Park as the best site for a possible ADA ramp. Construction for this project began on February 5. For questions about the project contact Gonzales at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: When Maryann Phelps tripped on the recently constructed bulbout on the corner of Oakland Avenue and El Cerrito Avenue, she didn’t remember falling. “It all happened so fast. I just went down,” she recalls. Phelps credits her fall to a small, threeinch raised curb on the northeastern bulb-out at that intersection which caught her foot as she tried to cross the street. A longtime resident of El Cerrito Avenue, she was at about 7:30 p.m. and barely noticed it in the evening darkness. After her fall, two strangers passing by helped her to her feet and walked her home, where her husband drove her to the fire station to be checked out. Phelps is currently recovering from an unrelated concussion and wanted to rule out the possibility of complications. “We were hoping the fire department would give us the okay to go home, but they didn’t,” said Phelps. Phelps spent Wednesday night, March 13, bouncing between hospital rooms in Alta Bates Summit Medical Center before her X-rays and CAT scans came back normal, and she left the hospital. The ordeal left her with scraped heel palms, a black eye and lingering pain in her jaw. Phelps said the current design of the bulb-outs poses a hazard and she would like to see more safety measures taken by the City to prevent trip-and-falls. “I’d just like to see something placed there before it happens to somebody else,” she said. articles.text: March is Women’s History Month, a time to celebrate and recognize the remarkable achievements and contributions of women throughout the past and present, and the role they play in inspiring future generations. Sally Ride made history on June 18, 1983, when she became the first American woman to travel to space. She was born in 1951 in Encino, California, and from a young age was fascinated by science. Her journey toward becoming an astronaut began at Stanford University, where she earned a Bachelor of Science in Physics and a Bachelor of Arts in English. She continued her education at Stanford, earning a Master of Science and a Doctorate in Physics. Towards the end of her academic career, she came across an advertisement for NASA’s astronaut program and decided to apply. In 1978 Ride joined the astronaut program. Out of 8,000 applicants, she was one of 35 individuals chosen and one of only six women selected. After years of training, she was assigned to the historic STS-7 mission. On June 18, 1983, Sally Ride embarked on the STS-7 mission aboard the space shuttle Challenger, making her the first American woman to travel to space and only the third woman in history to achieve this incredible milestone. The crew of five returned after a 147-hour mission. After this groundbreaking achievement, Sally Ride embarked on a second mission where she journeyed back into space in 1984 for an 8-day voyage. After leaving NASA in 1989, Sally Ride founded Sally Ride Science in 2001 to pursue her long-time “passion of motivating girls and young women to pursue careers in science, math, and technology” as explained by Sally Ride. Her remarkable accomplishments broke gender barriers and paved the way for future generations of women. She is an inspiration to many, encouraging them to believe in themselves and pursue careers in STEM. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a nonprofit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.

articles.text: Dedicated on September 24, 1948 in honor of Jean C. Witter, Jr., beloved son, star quarterback, respected team captain, Optimo Award winner and honor student at Piedmont High School from 1935-1938. Jean took his athletic talents to U.C. Berkeley where his blocked punt led the Bears to a 16-0 upset win over Stanford in the 1941 Big Game. He also played rugby all four years and captained the 1942 National Championship Cal rugby team. Upon graduation from Cal, Jean was commissioned as an Ensign, United States Naval Reserve, and assigned to the USS San Francisco. He courageously gave his life for freedom on November 13, 1942 during the Battle of Guadalcanal, one of the fiercest naval battles of WWII. His ship took forty-five major hits while inflicting severe damage to a Japanese task force with vastly superior firepower. The destroyer escort, USS Witter, was named in his honor.

articles.text: Minor damage inflicted on home, no injuries Tom Phelps woke up around 10 a.m. on Wednesday, March 13, and saw orange cones lined up on the street from his bedroom window. “I thought they must be fixing the curb,’” he recalled. “After my morning routine, I sat on the bed, looked out the window, and realized, holy vow, there’s a tree down there!” A significant portion of a cityowned tree on the sidewalk in front of his home had split off and fallen onto his front lawn and on his roof and rain gutter. The tree just narrowly missed the front room window. Workers from the Public Works Department were called to dispose of the tree. The tree was cut up, processed, and removed within half an hour of the workers’ arrival, and their lawn was once again empty by 1 p.m. Public Works attributes the tree’s fall to high winds in the area. “Anytime you have an urban forest, you’re always concerned A fallen tree lands on the Phelps roof and rain gutter, narrowly missing the window. about the health of your trees,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “I think Piedmont does a very good job of maintaining its trees. We trim around a thousand trees every year, and we just completed our tree survey. We’ve been having strong wind events recently, which caused this tree to fail unexpectedly.” Public Works attributes the city-owned tree’s fall to high winds in the area. articles.text: 5-game winning streak ends with 1-run loss to Archie Williams Piedmont’s baseball team beat both Hayward and St. Patrick before having a five-game winning streak interrupted by a 5-4 loss to Archie Williams in San Anselmo on Friday, December 15. The pair of victories were over Hayward, 15-7 at Humphries Diamond, and 8-6 against St. Patrick on Tuesday, December 12 in Vallejo. Piedmont put on a strong hitting display with home runs in each of the games. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos hit a two-run shot against St. Patrick, and Markos Lagios cracked homers against both Hayward and the Peregrine Falcons. “Batting leadoff, I usually try to get deeper in the count, but I’m trying to hit the ball. too. He threw a fastball and left it right over the plate,” Lagios said following the win over Hayward. It’s been a strong start to the season for Piedmont, giving coach Eric Olson one of the best starts in his years with the team, “We’re certainly happy with where we are,” said Olson. “The bats were alive, I’m super proud of the guys. We don’t have a huge team like last year, so everyone’s been playing,” The Highlander bats have been a major part of the team’s hot start, with 18 hits against Hayward, eight against St. Patrick, and five against Archie Williams. “We’re proving we’re one of the best teams in NCS, so we just have to keep swinging and producing,” Will Parker said. “Every win we’ve had just pushes us to our final goal, which is to win the North Coast Section,” added Diego Delventhal. The Highlanders have an exciting week ahead, They will play at Oracle Park in San Francisco, home of the Giants on Saturday, March 23, in the Dante Benedetti Invitational. Their game with University will be at 11 a.m. and three runs scored. Papahadjopoulos was 3-for-3 with a double, two RBIs, and three runs scored. Dando was 3-for-3 with a double, four RBIs and two runs scored. Dicke was 3-for-4 with three RBIs and two runs scored. Vo was 2-for-4 with a double, two RBIs and a run scored. Fresh man pitcher Sam Ragones got the win, throwing three innings with five strikeouts, and allowing one earned run and one hit. 15-7 win over Hayward After allowing three runs in the top of the first inning, Piedmont stormed back to lead 4-3 in the bottom half. The Farmers tacked on two more in the top of the second, 5-4, but Piedmont rallied to add six runs in the bottom of the third, four more in the next inning, and one more in the fifth. The third inning started with a double by Parker off the deep right-center field fence, followed by Papahadjopoulos going opposite field for a double of his own off the right field fence—scoring Parker. Dando put PHS ahead with a single, while Brandon Dicke had an RBI single to make it 7-5. After Vo then smashed a double over the left fielder’s head, Lagios smacked a one-out, threerun homer over the left field fence and into Wildwood Elementary park—10-5. Final stats: Lagios was 3-for-5 with a double, homer, three RBIs, and two runs scored. Delventhal was 2-for-5 with a run. Parker was 2-for-3 with a double, RBI, 8-6 victory over St. Patrick St. Patrick opened with a 2-0 lead, but PHS got to the front with a three-run bottom of the second and added one more the following inning. The Bruins tacked on two more in the top of the fifth, but Piedmont rallied to add four runs in the bottom of the fifth. St. Patrick added two more in the top of the sixth Piedmont’s four-run bottom of the fifth started with Krumins getting hit by a pitch, while Parker brought him all the way around from first on a double to center field. Next up was Papahadjopoulos, cracking a tworun homer to left field. Dando singled, then scored after Jack Meyjes reached first on an error, then advanced to second. Final stats: Parker was 1-for-4 with a double, RBI and run scored. Papahadjopoulos was 2-for-2 with a homer, two RBIs, and three runs scored. Dando was 3-for-3 with a double, RBI and two runs scored. Ellis Moss got the win with 4.1 innings pitched and six strikeouts. 5-4 loss to Archie Williams Both teams were tied 1-1 after the first inning, while Archie Williams piled on four runs in the bottom of the fourth. PHS fought valiantly in the top of the seventh and scored three runs to close the score to 5-4 deficit, but couldn’t put the tying run across. Trailing 5-1 entering the final inning, Shafer Dando reached first base on a dropped third strike, while Jordan Vo drew a walk. With two outs and two runners on, Lagios cracked a threerun homer in a 1-2 count over the left field fence. But that was it, with Archie Williams striking out the last batter. Final stats: Lagios went 1-for-4 with a home run, three RBIs, and a run scored. Parker went 2-for-3, Krumins was 1-for-3 with an RBI. articles.text: Staff Photos Lucas Smolko defeated Lick-Wilmerding’s top singles starter, but lost in a match with Alameda. King and Tenney lost in three sets, 6-1, 2-6, 10-8. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team wrapped up a productivity week by winning three matches in three days. They shut out Hayward 7-0 on Thursday, March 14 on the road, edged past North Coast Section rival Lick-Wilmerding 4-3 in San Francisco the previous day, and beat league opponent Alameda 5-2 on Tuesday, March 12 at home. “We are playing well, which is important as the season is getting into full swing,” coach Jim Landes said. 7-0 over Hayward Hayward only had six players available and forfeited No. 2 and No. 3 doubles. At singles, Brahma won by a clean 6-0, 6-0 sweep, while Tenney also won 6-0, 6-0 at No. 2. Siddharth won 6-1, 6-0 at No. 3 and Olsen won 6-1, 6-4 at No. 4. In the only doubles match, Fasteau and Maximo Miller won easily 6-0, 6-0. 5-2 over Alameda At singles, Ben Breber won at No. 2 in double-bagel shutout fashion, 6-0, 6-0. Nate Welch had an impressive 6-2, 7-6 (7-2) win at No. 3. Lucas Smolko lost 6-1, 6-1 at No. 1 to Mason Conlin, while Graham Alban fell 6-2, 6-4. “The highlight of the singles was Nate Welch win at # 3 against an opponent who became stronger as the match wore on. Nate hit some big serves and forehands and pulled out the match in straight sets,” Landes said. In doubles, Nick King and Monte Imburg paired at No. 1 for a 6-2, 6-3 win. At No. 2 Hunter Fasteau and Will Tenney won a close match in straight sets, 7-5, 7-6 (7-2), while Torsten Olsen and Kasper Jansson won 6-1, 6-4 at No. 3. 4-3 over Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont split its singles matches but won two of three doubles to win a close match with a North Coast Section rival. At singles, Smolko defeated Soahil Michra in straight sets, 6-1, 7-6 (7-3) at No. 1. Breber also won 6-1, 6-3 at No. 2, while Welch suffered a 6-2, 6-2 loss at No. 3 and Alban dropped No. 4, 6-2, 6-4. “Lucas and Ben both won their singles matches in straight sets. Lucas had a tight second set but clinched his match and the team’s victory by playing a great second set tiebreak. It might have been best match Lucas has played this season thus far,” Landes said. At doubles, Arun Brahma and Imburg won 6-1, 7-5 at No. 1. Fasteau and Jansson won at No. 3 in three sets, 5-7, 6-3, 10-8. At No. 2 was another close battle, where Arun Brahma won in tennis against Lick and Hayward.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team made a splash at the recent De La Salle invitational on Friday and Saturday, March 15-16, showcasing their talent against some of the area’s most skilled teams. Out of the 25 high school teams entered, the PHS boys’ team won 6th place and the girls’ team placed 8th overall. The high school team, still competing without a home pool, had 23 swimmers at the prelims and 11 reached the finals the next day. “There were a lot of new personal bests during Friday’s prelims. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team increased its winning streak to six matches with a 13-1 drubbing of Alhambra on Monday, March 18 in Martinez, 14-2 over Dougherty Valley on Friday, March 15 at Witter Field, and a surprising 11-4 beatdown of NCS power Novato on Tuesday, March 12. Of the group, Dougherty Valley is a Division 1 North Coast Section opponent, while Alhambra and Novato compete in Div. 2 which Piedmont was promoted to after last season. The Highlanders now look ahead to the start of their Western Alameda County Conference schedule, getting things started with a pivotal game with rival Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland. Piedmont has won six straight WACC titles over the Dragons. “We’re coming for Bishop O’Dowd, that’s all I’m going to say,” said senior Rylan Nelson confidently. 13-1 over Alhambra Piedmont only led 1-0 by the end of the first quarter, then exploded to lead 5-1 entering halftime. PHS piled on three more goals in the third and another five more in the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s Rylan Nelson scored the game’s first goal at the 8:19 mark of the first quarter. The match waged on with neither team scoring in the remaining time of the opening quarter. In the second, Alhambra scored to tie the match at 1-1 with 8:42 to go, but it marked the only time the Bulldogs got on the Staff Photos Piedmont’s new coach Jeff Lamb and the Highlanders are on a hot streak with six wins in a row. scoreboard. From there, Connor Fredericks scored with 6:46 remaining, Oliver Shafroth sent one in nearly two minutes later, then Curtis Hohener assisted Nelson on a goal with 1:09 left in the half, making it 5-1. Piedmont sent in three more goals in the third quarter, all coming by way of assists. Shaforth tossed one to Cairo Osman at 7:52, Osman then assisted Hohener on the very next possession 30 seconds later, then Nelson flicked a pass to Hohener to put the Highlanders ahead comfortably 8-1 with 5:26 left in the third. In the fourth, Fredericks won the faceoff and turned up field, leading to Hohener assisting Nelson just 24 seconds in at 11:36, Fredericks then scored 25 seconds later. Hohener assisted Nelson for another goal at 9:34 left, then Fredericks assisted Nelson 50 seconds later, while Nelson closed the game with another goal at 7:36 on an assist from Shafroth. Final stats: Nelson had six goals, one assist, and recovered two ground balls. Hohener had two goals, three assists, and scooped two ground balls. Osman had a goal and assist. Shafroth had two goals, two assists, won six faceoffs, and gathered eight ground balls. Fredericks had two goals, two assists, five ground balls, and won six faceoffs. Ethan Alering had seven ground balls. 14-2 over Dougherty Valley Piedmont led 4-1 by the end of the first quarter and 5-2 by halftime. The Highlanders then exploded for four goals in the third quarter and five more in the fourth without allowing another goal to DVHS. PHS had three players with 3-goal hat tricks. Rylan Nelson had six goals on Alhambra, three goals on Dougherty Valley, and four on Novato.

articles.text: Piedmont plays University at Oracle Park this Saturday. Saturday, March 23 marks an exciting day for the Piedmont baseball team and parents of the players. The Highlanders will play a game in the 2024 Dante Benedetti Classic against University at 11:30 a.m. in Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. It represents a rare opportunity to step onto the pro field at Oracle Park likely for the only time in their sporting careers. “It’s going to be a thrill for me, too,” said coach Eric Olson. I’ve played on some big league fields before but as a Giants fan, it’s going to be an amazing time. We’re really humbled to be asked to participate,” Unlike his young players, Olson remembers fondly the years at Candlestick with players like Will Clark. “I was a Will Clark guy. Growing up in the 80s, we had Will Clark. Those were the Candlestick years. It’s going to be a thrill, I’m going to be just as excited running out to be third-base coach as these guys are running out to the field,” Olson said. Will Parker, the Highlanders’ catcher, grew up as a Giants’ fan and goes to games with his teammate Markos Lagios, a Dodgers fan. “I grew up a Giants fan and am a big Buster Posey fan. I’m going to be able to catch that game where he played, so it’s going to be really fun. It’s tough going to games with Markos as a Giants fan, Everyone is always asking me why I’m hanging out with him, so I’ll pretend I don’t know him sometimes,” Parker said. “It’s like a dream. I’m going to try and soak it in as much as I can. I always go when they play the Dodgers. Growing up on this side of the Bay and playing a San Francisco team, it’s sort of like our Battle of the Bay. Will and I have gone to almost every Giants-Dodgers game when it’s here,” Lagios mentioned. Senior infielder Peter Krumins is also a Giants fan. San Francisco winning the World Series in 2010, 2012, and 2014 helped spur his fandom as a youngster. “I’ve been a Giants fan my whole life. They had the dynasty from 2010 to 2014, and I would go to Opening Day with my grandpa for six years in a row. My favorite memory was sometime in the playoffs when it was pouring rain, I remember sitting there in the stands when Marco Scutaro had a big hit, then raised his hands to the sky in the middle of the rain. That moment just stuck with me,” Krumins said. Sophomore second baseman Diego Delventhal is another Giants fan, but his favorite player Brandon Crawford is now with the St. Louis Cardinals. “I have pictured being on the field when I was four or five. Just being out there is going to be a lot of fun,” Delventhal said. Tickets to the event can be purchased on GoFan.co. Scan the QR code provided with your phone. articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco will open its newest exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World, on Saturday, April 6. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade. They highlight the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period was when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of Japan’s feudal military rule. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art, notably printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked both before and after the Meiji era. A museum member preview takes place on Thursday and Friday, April 4-5. A donor reception will be held on Thursday, April 11, from 7 to 9 p.m. The exhibition is on display at the Legion of Honor through August 18. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints. Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849), Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)

articles.text: Installation view of Zanele Muholi: Eye Me at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) first major exhibition on the West Coast of South African artist Zanele Muholi is now on view through August 11. The multimedia exhibition, entitled Zanele Muholi: Eye Me, features over 100 of the artist’s photographs from 2002 to the present alongside paintings, sculpture and video. Eye Me celebrates the artist’s Black queer community in post-Apartheid South Africa and showcases issues of gender identity, representation and race. Muholi was born in Durban and currently lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. The museum has featured works by Muholi in the past, including Faces and Phases in the 2011 exhibition Face of Our Time. Their work was also featured in Public Intimacy: Art and Other Ordinary Acts in South Africa, co-organized by SFMOMA and the Yerba Buena Center for Arts in 2014. To learn more and to purchase passes to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/zanele-muholi-eye-me/.
articles.title: SF MOMA features South African artist Zanele Muholi in new exhibit

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will conclude its Schwabacher Recital Series with an evening performance on Wednesday, April 3, featuring mezzo-soprano Samantha Hankey accompanied by pianist Carrie-Ann Matheson. The recital series offers audiences an opportunity to hear upcoming gifted singers in an intimate setting. Now in its 40th year, the series features renowned artists and has been instrumental in launching international careers. Hankey’s current season marks her debuts at the Royal Opera Covent Garden in London, where she performs as Dorabella in Così fan tutte; at Semperoper in Dresden as Cherubino in Le Nozze di Figaro; Detroit Opera as the Fox in The Cunning Little Vixen; and at Lyric Opera of Kansas City in the role of Santuzza in Cavalleria Rusticana. Hankey will be accompanied by pianist Matheson who currently serves as San Francisco Opera Center Program’s artistic director. The recital includes songs by Claudie Debussy, Manuel de Falla, Alexander Zemlinsky, Cole Porter and Kurt Weill. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. and takes place at the Taube Atrium Theater at 401 Van Ness Avenue next to the War Memorial Opera House. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/schwabacher-recital-series/. Mezzo-soprano Samantha Hankey

articles.text: Pulitzer prize finalist Lloyd Suh’s critically acclaimed new play The Far Country is now in performance at Berkeley Repertory Theatre with shows through Sunday, April 14. The Far Country follows Moon Gyet as he arrives at San Francisco’s Angel Island Immigration Station in the wake of the Chinese Exclusion Act with an invented biography and a new name. Moon, played by Tommy Bo, soon finds that passage to San Francisco, and the dream of a better life, comes with a price. “I’m incredibly proud to bring Lloyd’s beautiful play home to the Bay Area,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “It is an honor to share this story with our community, in this magical, complicated place that has inspired and compelled people from all over the world to leave their countries of origin to seek opportunity, safety, and home.” The cast includes Bo, Feodor Chin, John Keabler, Whit K. Lee, Tess Lina, Sharon Shao, and Aaron Wilton. A post-show discussion with Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation members and other panelists will be held on April 3 in Michael’s Second Act bar. The show is being performed at Berkeley Rep’s Peet’s Theatre, 2025 Addison Street in Berkeley. Purchase tickets by calling the box office at (510) 647-2949 or by visiting www.berkeleyrep.org.

articles.text: A scene from the Academy Award winning film The Zone of Interest The Zone of Interest, based on the 2014 book written by Martin Amis and directed by Jonathan Glazer, was the 2024 Oscar winner in the category of Best International Feature Film. The narrative opens with a silent, dark screen. Three minutes go by as if the audience is asked to abandon all extraneous thoughts and give themselves over to what will follow. And then the screen reveals an idyllic scene, a family, husband, wife, and children, seated on a blanket near a wide river, surrounded by tall summer grass. A sense of tranquility suffuses the day. Soon they all walk back to their car and drive home to a lovely manor house. Their day is ending, the children go to their rooms, and the parents crawl into twin beds, their conversation wanders before saying good night and turning out the bedside light. The next day, with the same sense of normalcy, the mother, Hedwig (Sandra Huller), with a toddler in her arms, walks out into the back yard, pausing to look at the blossoming flowers, the grass underfoot seems newly mowed, stone pavers lead to a small pool. The mother chats with the little one, smiling, encouraging the child to look at the surrounding plants. And it’s in this moment, a static, bucolic photograph, that the camera pulls back, allowing the audience to see more of what is a large and manicured garden awash in sunshine. And for the first time a massive concrete wall, topped with barbed wire, is revealed, and just beyond are brick buildings, several with rising smokestacks. The wall, stark, unexpected, forbidding, begs the question: why is it there? The answer is that this is the family home of Rudolf Hoss (Christian Friedel), the commandant of the concentration camp Auschwitch. And therein is the challenge inherent in watching this remarkable film. We are absorbed by all that we see, and simultaneously revolted by a dark, unfolding truth. It is that feeling which haunts every scene of The Zone of Interest thereafter. We watch in almost disbelief at the family’s quotidian, seemingly benign, normal life. Hedwig has other wives over for coffee and gossip. The dinner table is set. The kids are ever-present, often in the yard. Doors open and close. They pause for brief conversations. In one scene, Hedwig walks into her bedroom holding a mink coat, tries it on, and stands before a full-length mirror, happy, luxuriating in its warmth and richness. There is no hint that she ever wonders at its origin. Yet, if she listens, if she ever were to listen, screams and gunshots can be heard in the distance. Rudolf meets with a number of Nazi officers who look over architectural plans for an extermination building. They speak casually about meeting certain production quotas, comparing their Teutonic efficiency to other camps. It is evident that theirs is a congenial corporation of death offered up as business as usual. The family, to include a mother on a visit to see Hedwig, gushing with praise and pride, is surrounded by an unimaginable horror. But to the filmmakers, the impact of the film resides in the Barbara Riccardi and Dana Myers, violins; Jonna Hervig, viola; Nancy Bien, cello; Explore the development of the fugue form in classical music over a 300-year span, including the Beethoven Grosse Fuge , Op. 133, then enjoy the Brahms Piano Quintet, Op. 34.

articles.text: If you’re a fan of Woody Allen and have found delight in his ability to write and direct films set in Manhattan, framed by the central character’s existential plight (What purpose? What meaning?) and seasoned by his chronic hypochondria, then you will not be disappointed by Whatever Works. The film opens with an aging Boris Yellnikoff (Larry David), lapsed physics professor at Colombia, an almost winner of the Nobel Prize. He is a self-absorbed misanthrope, standing on a New York street reminding anyone who will listen that he’s surrounded by mental pygmies and inchworms. He also reminds all who will listen that his genius is unequaled and he is surrounded by the dimmest of bulbs. Having divorced his wife some years back (she was too wealthy and too smart), he attempted suicide in a moment of hopelessness and despair and was left with a limp. He now lives alone in a walk up in Chinatown. Unexpectedly, a young waif, Melody St. Ann Celestine (Evan Rachel Wood), appears at the foot of his stairs in need of shelter and a meal. Against all of his more selfish instincts, Boris agrees to let her stay one night. And so Melody, the quintessential inchworm, a mental pygmy personified, a retired beauty pageant winner from a small Southern town, always cheery and definitely clueless, gradually inserts herself into Boris’ life. Not surprisingly, they begin a relationship and Boris grows accustomed to having company, inchworm or no. The theme of older men and younger women, ripe with Pygmalion-Henry Higgins implications, threads itself through some of Allen’s work and it’s hard not to be reminded of Soon-Yi and the ensuing scandal when Allen married her (she was Mia Farrow’s adopted daughter that Farrow and Allen, for a time, raised together). Of course, though Larry David delivers a solid portrayal of Boris, it’s impossible not to see Woody Allen doing Boris’ standup rants while wondering why Allen didn’t play the role himself. The character is pure Woody to include moments when Boris wakes in the dead of night with a panic attack, screaming “the horror, the horror,” Boris being an unyielding fan of Conrad’s Kurtz in The Heart of Darkness. While Whatever Works may seem to be a flip title, akin to that insouciant, adolescent rejoinder, “whatever,” Boris’ explanation of those two words is poignant and then some. There are also laugh out loud moments to be sure, though the film lacks the complexity and subtlety of, say, Hannah and Her Sisters, Manhattan, or, more recently, Vicky, Cristina, Barcelona. The fact is that even when Woody is not quite at the peak of his game, he can still deliver a smart and funny film. Whatever Works. Directed by Woody Allen. Starring Larry David, Evan Rachel Wood, Patricia Clarkson and Ed Begley. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Streaming on VUDU/prime/apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs First things first: the kids will enjoy Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs, especially the return of Sid the Sloth, Manny and Ellie the wooly mammoths, Diego the saber-toothed tiger and, of course, Scrat the sort of squirrel. What is Scrat, really? It’s like asking if Goofy is a dog. Pluto yes, but Goofy? The movie opens with the irresistible Scrat in pursuit of that ever-elusive acorn. This time, the long-nosed sort of squirrel runs into a serious diversion in the form of Scratte, a foxy looking sort of squirrel. Their antics are inserted throughout the movie and eventually the acorn is forgotten – but that’s act three. Truth be told, for all of the attention given to Manny and company, Scrat has always had the most comic potential. The critter is funny. Sort of Road Runner funny. Anyway, as it turns out, Sid the sloth, wanting to start a family like Manny and Ellie (she’s pregnant and Manny is nervous) finds three large eggs, down in an ice cave. He wrestles them to the surface, the eggs hatch and surprise! The wee ones are three small T-rexes. That’s right, dinosaurs in the ice age (isn’t this the Pleistocene era?). And their mother is not happy when she discovers they’re gone. She grabs the three little guys plus Sid and heads home, which is a Mesozoic era jungle beneath the ice. Yep. Hot and humid below, frozen and cold above. The Ice Age gang goes looking for Sid, journeying into the land of the dinosaurs. The story may seem to unfold at a glacial pace but remember the designated audience is kids, and they love these characters There are the rascal twin possums; the aging Diego; Sid, Manny, and Ellie; and the new guy, Buck, a weasel who has lived in dinosaur land for too long. So, if time hangs heavy, days start to grow long, grab the kids and go. Or find it on streaming. Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs. Animation. Directed by Carlos Saldanha. The unfortunate thing is that so few on the West Coast have even heard of him. First and foremost, he is an outstanding representative of the Classic Russian school of piano playing. The second thing to keep in mind is that he is 89 years old, and still plays magnificently. I’d like to add that he is a man of great moral principle. Risking well-deserved peace in old age, he took a stand against Russian aggression and came to the United States at the ripe age of 87. An entire chapter could be written about his This column has noted many salubrious changes in music in recent years. Unfortunately, despite the positive trend, we have also seen a degradation of music education. And with this degradation of music education, there is a general degradation in education as a whole. Outstanding musicians like conductor David Morales are actively involved in rectifying these wayward trends. He is the founder and Artistic Director of Cantare, where he conducts Conductor Leo Eylar the 100-voice Cantare Chorale. Maestro Morales inspires as he goes. When I was a teacher in San Francisco public schools, I sometimes had as many as 1200 students a week. All of my students learned to read music and recognize every instrument of the orchestra by sight and by sound. In addition, they sang a large repertoire of songs, and became proficient playing the recorder. Please understand that these were the minimum things that we enjoyed. We also learned how to participate in music by being team players, and at the same time retaining our individual philosophies. These are very important aspects of music. articles.text: Come celebrate the 30th Anniversary Edition of Random Kindness and Senseless Acts of Beauty at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, March 22, at 7 p.m. Register in advance: https:// eventbrite.com/e/854973166757. The quartet will be joined in the second half by internationally-acclaimed pianist Carl Blake for the Brahms Piano Quintet, Op. 34. Pianist Carl Blake Temescal String Quartet: Barbara Riccardi and Dana Myers, violins; Jonna Hervig, viola; Nancy Bien, cello Carl Blake is a Bay Area classical pianist who has performed recitals to international acclaim in Carnegie Recital Hall in New York, Wigmore Hall in London, and the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia. He is a two-time recipient of Fulbright Scholar Awards and toured as Artistic Ambassador for the U.S. State Department to Brazil, Peru, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Honduras, Barbados and Jamaica. As they played, the listeners were drawn in, and by doing so we encountered the glory of the music as if we were members of a transcendental partnership. They solved all problems of balance. The strings spoke as an ensemble and for themselves. Dr. Blake was ever so sensitive. He has a velvet touch and an artist’s soul. It takes really special talent to express the innermost feelings of introspection and warmth of emotion.” The suggested donation at the door is $25 per person. Children and students are admitted free. Refreshments will be served following the concert.

The egg hunt will start rain or shine at 9:45 a.m. Right now they are stuffing thousands of eggs for all hunters. Spring-themed activities will be set up around the Park. There’s even an opportunity to have photos taken with the Springtime Bunny. Register online before the event. There is a $10 fee for age 3 and older. For older egg hunters who still love a good chase, an Eggstravaganza is happening at Piedmont Community Church this Saturday, March 23, from 5-7 p.m. There’ll be an egg hunt, face painting, crazy fun games and all free. –Abby Dear Abby: What are the healthiest dog breeds? My dear dog-friend Turk just passed and I would like to avoid that feeling for a while. He lived to be nine – 63 in dog years. Far too short. –Silvia Dear Silvia: I’m so sorry to hear about Turk. Getting a new puppy (or a new older dog) is definitely worth thinking through the health concerns that affect certain breeds. I’m not sure if you prefer a big or small dog, but here are the top three breeds to get you started. 1. Australian Cattle Dog – are seen occasionally around Piedmont. The Guiness Book of Records says the World’s Oldest Dog was an ACD named Bluey, who lived to the ripe age of 29 – that’s 203 in dog years. 2. Poodles – are not only hypoallergenic but they also tend to have long, healthy lifespans of up to 18 years, regardless of whether they are Standard, Miniature or Toy. Eye and joint issues tend to affect them in their older years. 3. Border Collies – tend to be lovable and vigorous and tend to be healthy for most of their lives which can go on average from 12-18 years. However deafness and epilepsy can affect them when they get long in the paw. Certain breeds like bulldogs are known to develop respiratory issues. Pugs can commonly suffer from eye infections. Frenchies, which were named the top US Dog Breed last year, can suffer from excessive itching and licking as well as respiratory issues. Mutts and Crossbreeds (like Queen E’s Corgi/Dachshund mix) are commonly thought to be healthier dogs than some Purebreds. But there is no guarantee that the dog you pick won’t develop something which turns into a hefty vet bill. Lots for you to chew on. –Abby If you have dog news, please send it to Melandogs@gmail. com. Abby would be most grateful to share your stories. E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@aol.com.

articles.text: Another large turnout of 42 walkers and one K-9 best friend showed up last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk on a lovely, clear morning. The walkers also checked out the progress on two bulb-out/sidewalk extenders at El Cerrito and Jerome Avenues now expected to be completed by the end of the month. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales expects they will make the area safer by increasing pedestrian visibility, shortening street crossings, and reducing vehicle speeds. articles.text: Author and journalist Bill Wong, a Piedmont resident, will celebrate the release of his new book “Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America” on March 24. At the book release, Wong will read selections from his memoir and discuss some life experiences with his perspectives as a journalist, a son, an Oakland native, and as an Asian-American. Wong will read primarily from the first chapter to set up the contrast between the eras, and locales in the book. The book launch will take place this Sunday, March 24 from 1:00-2:00 p.m. in the Oakland Asian Cultural Center, 388 Ninth Street in Oakland. This release of the memoir is the culmination of 13 years of work in which he discusses his roots and his identity. “Many Americans are curious about ancestral roots, whether they begin in Europe, Africa, Asia or Latin America,” said Wong. “I think the book should have appeal to people of many ethnicities. It’s my optimistic and cautionary ‘Thank you America’ tale,” he added. Wong was born in Oakland’s Chinatown to Chinese immigrants. The language spoken at home was Cantonese with his father’s dialect of Hoisan or Toisan. When Wong attended Lincoln Elementary School, he began his own journey with the English language. Although raised first with the language of his father, he only knew his father for 20 years of life. The book explicates how Wong grew out of Chinatown, psychologically, linguistically and physically, to become part of the American culture. “Wong’s memoir is more than a personal recounting; it is a bridge between past and present, offering insights into the challenges and triumphs of the Chinese-American community,” said the Breaking News Network (BNN). Wong graduated from Oakland High School and as a student at UC Berkeley he wrote for The Daily Californian. After his undergraduate studies he was with the Peace Corp in the Philippines and later graduated from the Columbia School of Journalism in New York in 1970. Wong’s first professional experience was with the San Francisco Chronicle as a general assignment reporter in the summer of 1962. He went on to Author and Piedmont resident Bill Wong. become a staff writer with the Wall Street Journal, from 1970- 1979, and joined the Oakland Tribune in 1979 where he spent 17 years on staff and then as a syndicated columnist. He was highly respected and well read, and became a regular contributor on The News Hour with Jim Lehrer on PBS in 1995 and 1996. Wong’s book features photos from a trip he and his sisters took to his father’s village in 1994. For Bill’s older sisters who grew up in China, the trip was a homecoming. But for Bill it marked a journey of complicated emotions and part of his search for identify. Seeing his father’s worn home in China proved to be an emotional experience. Bill describes his book as an immigrant success story. “But our society has deep issues; we are still deciding what kind of democracy we want to be,” Wong qualified. articles.text: There was a good turnout of 17 readers for the First Mondays Reading Group on Monday, March 4 at the Community Hall. The group was there to discuss Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis. This debut novel was first published in 1954 and won the 1955 Somerset Maugham Award for fiction. The story follows the academic and romantic pursuits of Jim Dixon, a history lecturer at an English university. The book is regarded by many as the finest, and funniest, comic novel of the twentieth century, but it scandalized readers in 1954. Time magazine included Lucky Jim in its 100 Best English-language Novels from 1923 to 2005. Dixon has had a rocky start at the university and is concerned about losing his position. He tries to maintain a good relationship with his absent-minded department head, Professor Welch, in order to be awarded a permanent post. Dixon also has a difficult relationship with a sometimes girlfriend who also teaches at the university. He meets Christine Callaghan, who is the latest girlfriend of Welch’s son. Dixon becomes attracted to her and they navigate their relationships. The story reaches its climax during an important lecture that Dixon is to give. However, he drinks too much in an attempt to calm his nerves, mocks the university’s culture, and passes out. Welch lets Dixon know his position at the university will not be extended, but all turns out well and he becomes Lucky Jim. The book generated strong feelings among the group. Some readers really enjoyed it, while others had a strong dislike. Some members had read the book years before, and their current reactions were different. They didn’t appreciate Amis’ satire, and they found Dixon to be unlikable. For that matter, they didn’t like or were interested in any of the characters. They weren’t funny. They were flawed, selfish and petty. Some readers couldn’t believe the book is considered one of the best of the 20th Century. The humor was juvenile, and they found the happy ending to be unrealistic. On the other side of the discussion were those who liked Lucky Jim and felt it was a brilliant satire of British society and academic life of the 1950s. It provided a picture of the post-World War II in England. The cigarette smoking and treatment of women seem to be artifacts. It was noted that England in 1954 was still recovering from the war, but ten years later the Beatles and mini-skirts appeared. Times change and this story presents a time and place that Amis satirizes and even mocks. Some readers marveled at Amis’ command of the English language and a vocabulary that required constant dictionary use Maya Angelou’s I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is the group’s April book. by the readers. Others would have preferred language that regular people could more easily understand. Some readers didn’t feel Dixon was a “jerk.” Rather, they saw him as a sometimes misbehaving, girlfriend-loyal, job-insecure young man, trying to keep his cushy academic job, and sort out his romantic life. Possibly the presentation of Amis’ Lucky Jim in a London West End theater with all his flawed characters and satire would be more universally appealing today. However, the book did provide another lively, fun First Mondays Reading Group discussion. The group had previously selected I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou for April and Perestroika in Paris by Jane Smiley for May. Three new, non-fiction candidates for June were considered and Prequel by Rachel Maddow was selected. The next discussion will be on April 1st (no joke) at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee. Registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. articles.text: In February Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 went on a backpacking and overnight camping trip to Point Reyes in West Marin. Before starting the hike, the Scouts had an opportunity to look through the Point Reyes Museum showing the diversity of the area and its many native species. After seeing the displays, the Scouts watched a short documentary film about the wildlife in Pt. Reyes National Seashore. The weather was beautiful and so was the hike. Many different thriving green plants could be found along the trail. A storm prior to the trip caused a number of trees to fall, blocking parts of the trail. Although it slowed the hiking, the trees proved to be a fun challenge to add to the approximately four-mile hike. After arriving at the campsite, everyone went to work setting up their tents and arranging their sleeping gear. There was not a After setting up camp, the Scouts hiked to the top of Point Reyes where they saw the elevation marker. Group photo of Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 at Pt. Reyes National Seashore. cloud in the sky, so it was a good time for taking a break and eat lunch. Then it was time to walk to the peak of Point Reyes. Some weren’t sure what to expect from the “peak” and it definitely wasn’t what some Scouts were imagining. Instead of scaling a mountain like at least one Scout had envisioned, they learned that the peak was a medium sized rock slightly raised above the ground. articles.text: It is with a profound sense of loss that the Goddard and DeVries families announce the passing of Bruce William Goddard at the age of 76. Bruce lost his battle with pulmonary fibrosis at his home in San Leandro, CA on March 10, 2024, while surrounded by his children and his dog, Geez. Bruce lived a remarkable life. Born Bruce William Goddard on May 6, 1947 at Merritt Hospital in Oakland, he was the son of Merle Goddard and Beverly Burger. He was a force of nature from the very start. Many of the eye-popping stories of hijinks from his childhood involved his siblings – Bob, Brian, and Brenda – who were sometimes collaborators and, at other times, victims. Bruce’s siblings Bob and Brenda preceded Bruce in death. Bruce is survived by his brother Brian, who is still owed from Bruce’s unfortunate losing position on their most recent bet. Bruce’s childhood formed his lifelong passion for politics, baseball, Americana music, and “Goddard humor.” He attended Oakland public schools, graduating from Skyline High School in 1964. He spent the next two years at Laney College in Oakland, where he was student body president and played wide receiver on Laney’s first-ever football team. Memorably, Bruce played a hard-fought game against a team of inmates inside San Quentin prison. Bruce then matriculated to UC Berkeley, earning a political science degree in 1969. Lifted by the spirit of the time and his determination to do good for the world, Bruce put his new degree to work with teaching jobs at “street academy” schools in New York and then Washington, DC. When his school folded, Bruce found himself in DC hard up for cash and a very long way from home. The circumstances led him to a taxicab career. He spent the next seven years driving a DC taxi, tending bar at DC clubs, traveling the world, and making lifelong friendships. The stories from his time in the nation’s capital have achieved legendary status. In retelling these stories, Bruce reminded us that “everyone who ever had a gun in my cab was mad at someone else, not me.” He became Dan Rather’s regular cabbie, a relationship that afforded Bruce a first-hand account of the unfolding Watergate scandal from one of the nation’s top newsmen. Later, a then-unknown singer named Emmylou Harris sang to Bruce backstage while he was tending bar at the DC club Reading Gaol. This is all not to be outdone, however, by one very strange and long night ending with a cup of coffee in, of all places, President Gerald Ford’s living room. As Bruce stared down the fast-approaching age of 30, he realized it was time to get back to his true love: politics. He moved back to the Bay Area, ran local political campaigns and moonlighted as a department store Santa Claus (“Sanity Clause”, a term he preferred.) In 1978, Bruce connected with Tom Bates, another Berkeley grad and ex-football player, on a mission to do some good. For the next decade, Bruce worked for the State Legislature as Assemblyman Tom Bates’ chief political lieutenant. Bruce was a fixture in the East Bay political scene for decades. Even when he wasn’t running a campaign, he was sought out for his sage political advice and candid observations. Those calls and requests for advice continued up until the week of his death. Most importantly, this was the time in which he met a fellow legislative staffer named Judy DeVries, whom he married in 1989. Judy brought her two children, Cisco and Will, into the blended family. Shortly thereafter, Caroline Goddard was born to Bruce and Judy. After a stint with AC Transit and earning a master’s degree in public administration from Cal State East Bay, Bruce joined the newly formed Alameda County Waste Management Authority, now known as StopWaste. Bruce’s political acumen, communication skills, and creativity were put to use in all manner of advertisements and campaigns focused on recycling and other environmental goals. The result was a significant increase in recycling and the emergence of one of the most influential environmental agencies in the State. His young daughter, Caroline, was often an uncredited star in the Authority’s TV spots. After retiring from the Authority, Bruce returned to his alma mater, Laney College, in 2007 – this time as an assistant to the college’s president, Dr. Frank Bruce Goddard, a former Piedmont resident, passed away on March 10, 2024. He was 76. Bruce Goddard is shown as a Piedmont High School softball coach. Chong. Even after departing the President’s office, he continued to serve as the Laney College football public address announcer, often supported in the press box by his grandchildren. H i s p s e u do -r e t i r e me nt involved a near full-time commitment to high school and college sports. Having served as the scorekeeper for the Piedmont High School softball team during his daughter Caroline’s time playing there, Bruce remained connected to the program and ultimately served as the assistant softball coach from 2014 - 2018. He also developed deep relationships with a number of women’s college basketball teams, often traveling the country with Cal, Pepperdine, USC, Long Beach State, the University of Washington, and others. Finally settling into full retirement, Bruce could focus more on music and travel. He played acoustic guitar sets for his neighbors during the COVID lockdown and recorded his own album, “Next to you, Next to me,” produced by Jeff Berkley, in 2021. He and his dog traveled the country on “Geez and the Geezer” road trips, making friends at every stop. Bruce was proud to have visited all 50 U.S. States, including 48 with Geez by his side. During his life Bruce chatted with Rickey Henderson, Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton, Jane Fonda, and Mikhail Gorbachev. He left an indelible mark on East Bay politics, sports, and colleges. His lousy jokes will continue to be told for generations. But most importantly, he was a dedicated father and grandfather to a family whose interests and passions are directly influenced by him. Daughter Caroline, Cisco, Will, Judy, his grandchildren Mateo, Mac, Ollie, Drew, and Lula, and Brian and Geez, and a long list of great friends already miss him and his sense of humor. The family will hold a private memorial at a date to be determined.

articles.text: On their latest excursion, the Piedmont Seniors explored the world from the heart of Golden Gate Park at the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Among the areas they visited were a self-guided tour of the Osher Rainforest, the Kimball Natural History Museum, and Steinhart Aquarium followed by a tantalizing lunch at the Terrace Cafe and then a visit to the Morrison Planetarium. It had been several years since the Seniors’ last visit and they were eager to return. Upon arrival, the Seniors were met at the entrance by a courteous employee, who helped the group escape from the copious amounts of school children. She directed the Seniors to the Osher Rainforest, where the Seniors began their day’s exploration. Inside the dome of the Osher Rainforest, they were treated to a magnificent neotropical rainforest stretching 90 feet above, a lush, four-story rainforest that’s teeming with life, including live plants and. animals – everything from free-flying butterflies to exotic reptiles, amphibians, birds, and even a slithering Amazonian tree boa. The rainforest’s living plants include trees like the Brazilian beauty leaf and West Indies mahogany, dozens of shrubs, and hundreds of flowering plants from begonias and philodendrons to orchids, bromeliads, and even a rare corpse flower. The past, present, and future of life on Earth came alive for the Seniors through hands-on exhibits at the Kimball Natural History Museum, which features fascinating specimens, and a peek into the latest research conducted by the Academy’s scientists. The highlight was that of a towering T. rex in the main lobby. Another favorite was an albino Alligator mississippiensis that’s become one of the Academy’s most famous residents. The alligator, known as “Claude,” is part of an exhibit known as “The Swamp”, highlighting ecosystems of the Southeastern United States. The Piedmont Seniors then explored the world’s most vibrant, virtual ecosystems at the Steinhart Aquarium, one of the most biologically diverse and interactive aquariums in the world. Home of nearly 60,000 live animals, representing more than 1,000 unique species, Steinhart Aquarium offers an unprecedented view of underwater and terrestrial habitats, from species displayed nowhere else in the world to exhibits about cutting-edge research in little-known ocean ecosystems. The visit was definitely filled with discovery. At lunchtime, the group headed to the Terrace Café, where the food was delicious, the service impeccable, and the ambiance couldn’t be better. The seniors were seated indoors with all glass walls to offer a panoramic view of the luscious outdoor gardens. The “sous chef” came out to introduce herself and to meet and greet the Piedmont Seniors. The next visit at the Academy of Sciences was to the Morrison Planetarium for a half-hour production. The 75-foot dome immerses the audience inside cutting-edge visualizations and hyper-realistic virtual environments. From faraway galaxies to the workings of our own planet, the Piedmont Seniors experienced the cosmos like never before. But that wasn’t all. After their visit the Seniors boarded a bus to come home. articles.text: Tom Kelly (left), Jane Kelly, Park Commission Vice-Chair Kimberly Moses, Park Commissioner Arden Hall, Sara Gaucher, Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent, Park Commissioner Dave Johnson, and Tom Gandesbery volunteered to plant native riparian saplings at Bushy Dell Creek last week. On Thursday, March 15 ten volunteers — including five members of the Park Commission — gathered with Public Works staff to plant 40 riparian plants along Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park. Volunteers planted saplings of five different species, including Buttonwillow, California Box Elder, California Wild Rose, Oregon Ash, and White Alde. All are expected to thrive according to Park ComPark Commission Chair Tom Smegal and Tom Gandesbery planting saplings by Bushy Dell Volunteers Sara Gaucher and Tom Kelly planting saplings by the creek. mission Vice-Chair Kimberly Moses and Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent. “We had the opportunity because Watershed Nursery in Richmond had overstock from a project that had been delayed and they didn’t want the plants to go to waste,” explained Moses. “I thought of our ivyladen Bushy Dell Creek and on the off-chance that I could get permission from the City, I took Watershed up on the offer. Lucky for us Nancy [Kent] and the city maintenance crew accommodated our volunteer effort.” Moses added that the offer came at an opportune time in the season. Riparian plants usually thrive near streams or river banks. A little later and the summer drought would have made such a planting “impossible.” Volunteers at the event included commissioners Kimberly Moses, Tom Smegal, Arden Hall, Jack Fishrup, Barbara Giuffre, and Dave Johnson, as well as community members Tom Gandesbery, Sara Gaucher, and Tom and Jane Kelly. “This was a very small project, a sort of ‘proof of concept’ for volunteers to be allowed to plant riparian native plants in the park,” said Moses. “If we could work on educating dog owners about managing their pets near urban creeks, we could even clear ivy, acacia and privet from the creek and replace the invasive species that dominate it with beautiful native sycamore, alder and big leaf maples. Maybe even bring in some native California azalea!” For more information about the project or how to get involved with similar volunteering opportunities, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov.
